description: We are enthusiastic individuals who seek not only to learn and explore, but also to make a difference in our country. We pursue goals, embrace challenges, and find ways to support one another, because we believe we are never alone as long as we have each other. We are resilient, proactive, curious, and versatile. Whenever a question arises, nothing can stop us from finding the answer.
summary: Abyss began with something personal: one of our teammates lost many of his belongings during flooding in Honduras. His experience inspired us to build a web platform prototype that makes environmental information easier to understand and use. Through an interactive map, users can explore nine areas of Honduras, compare historical satellite indicators, examine rainfall scenarios, and download reports. Our goal is to help local authorities identify places that need closer inspection and make better use of limited resources. The current prototype uses preloaded datasets and illustrative calculations, with future work focused on connecting live services and validating results with specialists and field observations. By bringing this information together, we hope to support better preparation, guide levee inspections, and help communities facing recurring floods. Behind every point on the map is a family, and our motivation is to help others avoid the severe losses our teammate experienced.
details:
Abyss started with a story close to our team. One of our teammates lost many of his belongings during flooding in Honduras. Hearing what he went through made us ask how we could help communities prepare and give local teams better information about where to inspect first.

We built a web platform prototype that brings information about nine areas of Honduras into one interactive map. Users can explore places such as Chamelecón, Rivera Hernández, Cofradía, and the Ulúa River, compare observations across different dates, and view historical radar and optical water indicators. Charts make it easier to follow changes over time and see when optical observations are missing.

The app also lets users try rainfall scenarios, explore illustrative projections from 6 to 12 days, and download PDF reports. A comparison index combines several indicators to highlight differences between areas. These results still need validation; they do not confirm that a levee is safe or predict the probability of a flood. The dashboard is available in Spanish and English, with three visual themes.

We developed Abyss with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used Tailwind CSS for the layout, Leaflet and Esri imagery for the map, Chart.js for the graphs, and jsPDF with AutoTable for reports. The current version runs in a browser with preloaded data. Connecting live satellite and weather services is part of our next stage.

What makes Abyss creative is how it brings maps, historical comparisons, scenarios, and reports together around a practical local need. We thought about cloudy weather, missing data, readability, and the limited time and resources inspection teams have. Our next steps are to verify data sources, explore NISAR deformation analysis, and work with specialists to check results in the field. We hope Abyss can support better inspection and maintenance decisions, so families like our teammate's have a better chance to prepare before the next flood.
